title: Writing for code review and software
text:
Software projects depend on short documents:

pull requests
issues
commit messages
READMEs
code comments
release notes

Readers of these documents often arrive without context on the change, so the rules in the other chapters apply to them too. This chapter lists the general rules that matter most here and adds a few that belong to software.

1 Apply the general rules

Write in the active voice and name the actor before the action.
Limit complex sentence structures: write one main idea per sentence and avoid piling several subordinate clauses into one.
Cut filler and prefer plain words (Word choice).
Scan for clichés before you post non-trivial prose. Skip the scan for code, terse status lines, and short replies, which are too short to contain a cluster of tells.
Put lists in bullet points.



2 Say what changed and why

Open a pull request description with the behavior a reader would see before and after the change.
Explain the reason for the change in the commit message, not only the content of the diff.
State what you checked and what you did not.
Link the issue, the data, or the document that motivates the change.


❌ Update plotting code.
✅ Label the y-axis in original units, so the figure no longer shows log-odds.



3 Decide writing style here, not by imitation
The repo maintainers make each writing-style decision explicitly and record it in this book. Take a writing-style choice from this book, not from the prose around your edit. A neighboring page shows what someone wrote once, not what the maintainers decided. When this book does not say how to write something, raise the question as an issue on psw, with your recommendation, instead of copying a nearby page. Code style follows the same rule in psc.


4 Comment code sparingly

Write a comment that says why the code does what it does, and let the code say what it does.
Keep each comment as short as it can be while still giving the reason.
Update or delete a comment when the code changes.



5 Check CRAN before you name an R package
Before you propose a name for an R package, check that nobody already uses it. Search these places, and report the result with the name:

the package page on CRAN, at https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/<name>/index.html, which returns 404 when the name is free;
the CRAN archive, at https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/<name>/, because a removed package still holds its name;
Bioconductor.

A name that CRAN has used is usually unavailable for a new package and confuses users, so pick a different name.


6 Write release notes for the user

Describe each change by its effect on the user, not by the file that changed.
Put breaking changes first, because the user must act on them.



7 Nest document source files by heading level
Split a long Quarto document into files that follow its headings:

The page file holds the YAML header, the macros include, every first-level heading, and an include of the body of each first-level section.
A section body holds that section’s second-level headings, and an include of the body of each subsection.
Continue the same way at each deeper level.
A file holds the headings nested below its own section’s heading, never that heading itself, so no file only adds one heading to one include.

Readers and reviewers then find the outline in one place, and an author edits each file as a unit. Apply the structure to a page when you edit it, and leave pages you are not editing as they are.










 Back to top

title: Paper organization
text: Effective organization helps readers navigate your scientific paper and understand your findings. The structure of your paper should guide readers logically from your research question through your methods to your results and conclusions.

title: Paper organization
text:
3.1 Single outcome studies
When analyzing a single primary outcome, organize results by:

Descriptive statistics first
Main analysis results
Sensitivity analyses or subgroup analyses

title: Paper organization
text:
3.2 Multiple outcomes analyzed separately
When analyzing multiple outcomes separately, group your results section by outcome rather than by analysis type. This organization improves clarity and readability by keeping all information about each outcome together.

3.2.1 Why group by outcome
Grouping by outcome helps readers:

Follow the story of each outcome from descriptive statistics through final results
Compare findings across outcomes more easily
Understand the complete picture for each outcome before moving to the next
Navigate directly to outcomes of interest



3.2.2 How to organize by outcome
For each outcome, present:

Descriptive statistics
Main analysis results
Sensitivity analyses
Subgroup analyses (if applicable)

Structure:
Results
├── Outcome 1: Mortality
│   ├── Descriptive statistics
│   ├── Main analysis
│   ├── Sensitivity analyses
│   └── Subgroup analyses
├── Outcome 2: Hospital readmission
│   ├── Descriptive statistics
│   ├── Main analysis
│   ├── Sensitivity analyses
│   └── Subgroup analyses
└── Outcome 3: Quality of life
    ├── Descriptive statistics
    ├── Main analysis
    ├── Sensitivity analyses
    └── Subgroup analyses


3.2.3 What to avoid
Don’t group by analysis type when outcomes are analyzed separately: 
Results (POOR ORGANIZATION)
├── Descriptive statistics
│   ├── Mortality
│   ├── Hospital readmission
│   └── Quality of life
├── Main analyses
│   ├── Mortality
│   ├── Hospital readmission
│   └── Quality of life
└── Sensitivity analyses
    ├── Mortality
    ├── Hospital readmission
    └── Quality of life
This forces readers to jump back and forth between sections to understand the complete story for any single outcome.


3.2.4 Exception: Shared descriptive statistics
If your descriptive statistics apply to all outcomes (for example, baseline characteristics in a clinical trial), present them once at the beginning before discussing individual outcomes.

title: Paper organization
Paper organization
text:
4.2 Captions are captions, not headings
Give every figure and table a numbered caption, including those in the supplementary material. A table without a caption is incomplete, even when its contents are correct.
Attach each caption to its figure or table with your writing tool’s caption feature (in Quarto, the last line of a #fig- or #tbl- div), not as a section heading.
Poor caption: a section heading that reads “Supplementary Figure S43: Distribution of follow-up time”, placed above the figure
Better caption: “Distribution of follow-up time”, written as a caption attached to the figure, with its label and number generated by your writing tool rather than typed by hand (a supplementary “S” prefix may need extra setup in the tool)
A heading posing as a caption usually appears in the table of contents, takes on heading styling, and is not attached to its figure. Its number is typed by hand, so it falls out of step with the real numbering when figures are added, removed, or reordered.

title: Paper organization
text:
4.3 Manuscript layout for journal submission
Many journals ask for figures and tables to follow the main text of a submitted manuscript rather than appear inline. Unless the journal’s instructions say otherwise, lay out a submission manuscript as follows:

Put all main-text figures and tables at the end of the main manuscript, after the main text and the references, and before the supplementary material. The main text still cites each one by number.
Insert a page break before the supplementary material header, so the supplement starts on a new page.
Keep each caption with its figure or table. Insert a page break before the first figure or table and between consecutive ones, so that each one starts on a page where it fits with its caption. Do not let a caption fall on a different page from its figure or table, or split across a page break, unless it cannot be avoided, as when a figure or table and its caption together are taller than a full page.

In Quarto, the {{< pagebreak >}} shortcode inserts a page break in PDF and Word output, and a ::: {#refs} div places the references where you put the div instead of at the end of the document. Write the figures and tables after that div.

title: Paper organization
text:
4.4 Check the rendered layout
Captions, page breaks, and figure placement are properties of the rendered document’s layout. Problems with them are easy to miss when reading the source, and a check of the text and numbers alone will not catch them. Before calling a rendered manuscript reviewed, page through the PDF or Word output and check its layout, not only its text and numbers:

Does every figure and table have a numbered caption?
Does each caption sit on the same page as its figure or table?
For a journal submission, do the main-text figures and tables come after the references and before the supplement, and does the supplementary material start on a new page?

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.
A mathematical paper is made of sentences, and the formulas are part of the sentences. This chapter collects rules for fitting formulas into prose. It draws on the lecture notes of a Stanford course on mathematical writing (Knuth et al. 1987). This chapter selects the rules that bear most on formulas. Several of the course’s other rules appear in other chapters, and Table 1 points to them. The notes also cover spelling, punctuation and refereeing, which this book does not.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
text:
1.1 Separate formulas with words
Put words between two formulas. Without them, the reader cannot tell where one formula ends and the next begins.







Example 1 (Separating two formulas)  

❌ Define \(f_k\), \(k \ge 2\).
✅ Define \(f_k\), where \(k \ge 2\).

In the ❌ version the comma between the two formulas seems to belong to the first one. The ✅ version names the relation between them.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
section: 1.2 Do not start a sentence with a symbol
text:
1.2 Do not start a sentence with a symbol
A sentence that starts with a symbol is hard to see as a new sentence, because the formula runs on from the period before it. Start with a word, such as the name of the object.







Example 2 (Starting a sentence with a word)  

❌ \(t^2 - 5\) has two real roots.
✅ The polynomial \(t^2 - 5\) has two real roots.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
text:
1.3 Write logical symbols as words
In prose, write “implies”, “for every” and “there exists”, not \(\Rightarrow\), \(\forall\) and \(\exists\). The same goes for the symbols for “therefore” and “such that”. Keep the symbols in a work on logic.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
section: 1.4 Test the sentence with the formulas removed
text:
1.4 Test the sentence with the formulas removed
Many readers skim past the formulas on a first reading. Replace each formula by a placeholder such as “blah”. If the sentence no longer reads smoothly, rewrite it.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
text:
1.5 Tie formulas together with commentary
A list of formulas with no words between them is the style of a homework paper. Say what each step does and why the next one follows. A sentence such as “Because the set \(S\) has an element, we can pick one and call it \(s\)” tells the reader where the argument is going, and the bare formula does not.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
section: 1.6 Make the prose say what the formula says
text:
1.6 Make the prose say what the formula says
The sentence that introduces or interprets a formula must describe that formula. Check every term in the sentence against the formula, symbol by symbol. The words and the symbols must name the same quantity, the same data, and the same kind of average. When you change one, change the other in the same edit.







Example 3 (A sentence that names the wrong average) Suppose the formula is \(\E{\paren{\newoutvar - \predvalf{\predvar}}^2}\), a population mean at one covariate value \(\predvar\). The sentence “the average squared error over the training set” does not describe it. It names a sample average over many observations. Write “the expected squared prediction error at \(\predvar\)” instead.




Before you submit, reread each formula next to the sentence that describes it. Do the same after every edit to either one. Related rules cover using one notation for one thing and defining every variable when you introduce it.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
section: 1.7 Write each sentence in words or in math, not both
text:
1.7 Write each sentence in words or in math, not both
A sentence is either entirely in words or entirely in math. A single inline expression inside a word sentence is fine, as in “the prediction function \(\predfn\) equals the conditional mean”.  A sentence that states one condition in words and a second condition as a relation between expressions is a hybrid. Split it into two complete sentences: the first states the result in words, and the second states it as a displayed formula.







Example 4 (Splitting a hybrid sentence)  

❌ The reducible risk is zero if and only if \(\P(\predfnf{\Predvar} \ne \E{\Outvar \mid \Predvar}) = 0\).
✅ The reducible risk is zero if and only if the prediction function differs from the conditional mean with probability 0. 
\[
\ba
\E{\sqf{\condE{\Outvar}{\Predvar} - \predfnf{\Predvar}}} &= 0
\\
\iff \Pf{\predfnf{\Predvar} \ne \condE{\Outvar}{\Predvar}} &= 0
\ea
\]

The ❌ version puts the first condition in words and the second in math. The ✅ version says the result once in words and once in math.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
section: 1.8 Give every relationship stated in words a formal expression

title: Introduction
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.


This book is a style guide for writing in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Most of its examples come from statistics and data analysis, because statistics and data analysis are the fields that I work in. Most of its rules apply to any writing that explains technical ideas.

1 What the book covers
Most chapters give rules for every kind of technical writing, such as a paper or a set of lecture notes. Four chapters cover one kind of document:

Paper organization and Preparing a manuscript for submission cover research papers.
Writing for teaching covers lecture notes, slides, and problem sets.
Writing for code review and software covers pull requests, issues, commit messages, READMEs, code comments, and release notes.



2 Who the book is for
I wrote this book for students and mentees who are learning to write about their research. I also wrote it for the AI writing assistants that draft and edit prose for me.
Many rules are stated as checks that a reader can apply to a single sentence, so a student and an AI assistant can apply them the same way. For example, the section on demonstrative pronouns asks whether each “this” or “that” is followed by the noun that it refers to. A person or a program can answer that question without knowing what the paper is about.


3 The principle behind the rules
The rules in this book apply one idea from the philosopher Paul Grice. Grice observed that people in a conversation expect each contribution to serve the purpose of the exchange (Grice 1975). He called this expectation the cooperative principle, and he divided it into four maxims (Davis 2024):

Quantity: be as informative as required.
Quality: say only what you believe true and can justify.
Relation: be relevant.
Manner: be clear, which includes avoiding obscurity and ambiguity, being brief, and being orderly.

A reader of technical writing expects the same cooperation from the author. A sentence that breaks a maxim makes the reader stop and guess what the author meant. Most rules in this book name one way to break a maxim and the fix.
The chapters serve the maxims as follows:

Quantity:

“Not more than required”: Conciseness.
“Not less than required”: Defining terms clearly and the sections of Word choice on naming the object a sentence refers to and following an abstract statement with an example.

Quality: Citations and evidence, which asks for support for each claim and for checking each source, and Avoiding clichés.
Relation: the sections of Conciseness on writing about the ideas and not about the document, and the layout of the Results section in Paper organization.
Manner:

Obscurity: Word choice.
Ambiguity: Grammar.
Brevity: Conciseness.
Order: the sections on assumptions first in Mathematical notation, on forward references in Paper organization, and on giving the general definition before examples in Defining terms clearly.


The maxims describe what a reader expects. They are not a checklist, because whether a sentence is relevant or informative enough depends on the reader and the purpose of the document. This book therefore states each rule as a check that does not depend on the reader, as the previous section describes, and uses the maxims to explain why each rule exists.


4 How the book is organized
The chapters fall into six groups:

Terms, notation, and evidence: 

Defining terms clearly
Mathematical notation
Citations and evidence

Papers:

Paper organization
Preparing a manuscript for submission

Words and sentences:

Word choice
Avoiding clichés
Writing for every reader
Grammar
Conciseness

Teaching:

Writing for teaching

Software:

Writing for code review and software

Thinking:

Writing to clarify your thinking


The Summary lists the book’s main rules as a checklist for revising a draft.


5 How to read the book
You can read the chapters in any order. Most sections state one rule and the reason for it, and then show the rule applied to an example. Many sections compare a weaker version of a passage with a stronger one. For example, the Word choice chapter recommends “before” over “prior to”:

❌ Prior to fitting the model, we removed outliers.
✅ We removed outliers before fitting the model.

Definitions, examples, and exercises appear in numbered, colored boxes, so that other sections and other documents can link to them.
Use the book as a reference while you write, and use the Summary checklist when you revise.


6 Further reading
These shorter guides cover some of the same ground:

Novelist Cormac McCarthy’s tips on how to write a great science paper (Savage and Yeh 2019)
Elements of style (Nature Physics 2007) - a Nature Physics editorial on scientific writing
The Pathway to Publishing: A Guide to Quantitative Writing in the Health Sciences (Luby and Southern 2022)
Secret, actionable writing tips - a thread on X

For who counts as an author, see the ICMJE criteria in Preparing a manuscript for submission.






NoteSource





This list traces back to the Benjamin-Chung Lab Manual by Jade Benjamin-Chung.



For further reading, see the Resources chapter of the UCD-SERG lab manual.


7 Contributing
The book is a work in progress. If a rule is unclear, wrong, or missing, open an issue on the book’s GitHub repository.

Grice, H. Paul. 1975. “Logic and Conversation.” In Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts, edited by Peter Cole and Jerry L. Morgan. Academic Press.

title: Grammar
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.


Clear grammar removes friction between your ideas and your reader. This chapter collects a few grammatical habits that consistently make scientific writing easier to read.

1 Relative pronouns
Relative pronouns introduce a clause that describes a preceding noun. The relative pronouns are:

that
which
who
whom
whose

Two habits make these clauses easier to read: choosing between that and which correctly, and keeping the relative pronoun rather than dropping it.

1.0.1 Restrictive vs. non-restrictive clauses: that vs. which







Definition 1 (Restrictive clause) A restrictive clause is a relative clause that identifies which thing you mean, and that cannot be removed without changing the meaning of the sentence.











Definition 2 (Non-restrictive clause) A non-restrictive clause is a relative clause that adds information the reader does not need in order to know which thing you mean.




Use that for a restrictive clause. Use which, set off by commas, for a non-restrictive clause.







Example 1 (Restrictive clause (that))  

The dataset that we collected in 2023 contains 4,000 records. 

The clause “that we collected in 2023” tells the reader which dataset we mean. Removing it changes the meaning, so the clause is restrictive and takes that with no comma.











Example 2 (Non-restrictive clause (which))  

Our 2023 dataset, which contains 4,000 records, is publicly available. 

The clause “which contains 4,000 records” adds a detail, but the reader already knows which dataset we mean. The clause is non-restrictive, so it takes which and is set off by commas.




A quick test: if you can drop the clause without changing which thing you are describing, use which and commas; otherwise, use that.


1.0.2 Do not omit relative pronouns
English lets you drop a relative pronoun in some sentences, but keeping it makes the structure of the sentence explicit and easier to parse on the first read. Prefer to keep that, which, or who, even when the grammar would let you drop it.







Example 3 (Restoring an omitted relative pronoun)  

❌ This body of work laid the methodological groundwork I now apply to enteric fever.
✅ This body of work laid the methodological groundwork that I now apply to enteric fever. 

The word “that” signals immediately that a describing clause is beginning, so the reader does not briefly misread “the methodological groundwork I” as a single phrase and then have to backtrack.







2 Demonstrative pronouns
There are four demonstrative words:

this
that
these
those

They can serve two roles. As adjectives, they modify a noun: “this result”, “those samples”.  As standalone pronouns, they replace a noun: “This shows…”, “That means…”. 
When a demonstrative stands alone as a pronoun, the reader has to search backward for its referent — and often the referent is a whole preceding clause rather than a single noun, which leaves the reference ambiguous. Prefer to follow a demonstrative with the noun it points to, so the reference is explicit. The adverbs here and there point the same way: “getting there” leaves the reader to guess where “there” is.
A demonstrative at the end of a sentence has no room after it for a naming noun, so a bare sentence-final this or that always leaves its referent unnamed. End the sentence with the noun instead.







Example 4 (Naming the referent)  

❌ The model overfit the training data. This poses a problem for deployment. 
✅ The model overfit the training data. This overfitting poses a problem for deployment. 
❌ The first model’s estimates were biased upward. The second model avoids this. 
✅ The first model’s estimates were biased upward. The second model avoids this bias. 

Adding the nouns “overfitting” and “bias” states exactly what each “this” refers to, instead of leaving the reader to infer it. The second pair ends its sentence with the demonstrative, so the fix has to add the noun after it, at the very end.






3 Quantifiers used as pronouns
Words that say how many, or how much, of something cause the same problem as demonstratives when they stand alone in place of a noun. Grammars call these words quantifiers, and call a quantifier that stands alone an indefinite pronoun. The common ones are:

both
all (and counted forms such as all three)
each
any
some
most
many
few
none

Every belongs to the same family, but it cannot stand alone (“every” needs a noun, as in “every model”), so it never causes this problem.
You do not need a complete list of quantifiers to apply the advice. Whenever a quantifier stands where a noun should be, the reader has to search backward to find out what it quantifies. Follow the quantifier with the noun: “both models”, “all three estimators”, “each interval”.  An “of” phrase that names the noun works too: “none of the intervals”. 







Example 5 (Naming what a quantifier refers to)  

❌ We fit a linear model and a spline model to the 2019 and 2020 surveys. Both return the same fit.
✅ We fit a linear model and a spline model to the 2019 and 2020 surveys. Both models return the same fit. 

In the first version, “both” could mean the two models or the two surveys. Adding “models” settles which pair the sentence is about.






4 Avoid garden-path sentences
A garden-path sentence leads the reader into one reading and then forces them to go back and reread when the rest of the sentence does not fit (Wikipedia: Garden-path sentence). The sentence may be grammatical, but the reader parses it twice.
A common cause of garden-path sentences in technical writing is a clause that describes a noun but has lost its opening that or that were. Without the pronoun, the reader takes the noun and the start of the clause as one phrase and has to reattach the words that follow. Do not omit relative pronouns gives the general rule.
When you reread a sentence and stumble, find the point where your first reading went wrong, and rewrite the sentence so that the first reading is the right one.







Example 6 (Rewriting a garden-path sentence)  

❌ Report only SHAs a command you ran printed in full.
✅ Report only SHAs that appeared in full in the output of a command that you ran.

In the first version, the reader takes “SHAs a command you ran” as one phrase, then reaches “printed” and has to work out that “a command you ran printed in full” is a clause describing the SHAs. The rewrite marks the clause with “that” and keeps each verb next to its own subject.






5 Name the object of a relational noun
Some nouns name a relation, so they are incomplete without the thing they relate to. Relational nouns include:

cause (of what?)
effect (of what, on what?)
reason (for what?)
result (of what?)
example (of what?)

When one of these nouns appears without its “of” or “for” phrase, the reader has to recover the missing object from context, just as with a pronoun that has no clear referent. Write the object next to the noun.







Example 7 (Comparing four versions of one sentence) Each version tries to say what usually causes garden-path sentences.


A common cause in technical writing is a clause that describes a noun but has lost its opening that or that were.
In technical writing, a common cause is a clause that describes a noun but has lost its opening that or that were.
In technical writing, a common cause of garden-path parsing is a clause that describes a noun but has lost its opening that or that were.
A common cause of garden-path sentences in technical writing is a clause that describes a noun but has lost its opening that or that were.


Versions 1 and 2 never say what the clause causes, so the reader has to look back to find what “cause” refers to. Version 3 names the object, “garden-path parsing”, but its fronted phrase delays the subject (see Lead with the subject), and “garden-path parsing” introduces a second term for the “garden-path sentences” that the section defines. Version 4 names the object, uses the defined term, and starts with the subject.






6 Appositive fronting
An appositive is a noun phrase that renames or describes the noun beside it. In “Bovine respiratory disease (BRD), a disease complex with a multifactorial etiology, kills calves”, “a disease complex with a multifactorial etiology” is an appositive of “BRD”. Appositive fronting moves the appositive to the start of the sentence, before the noun it describes, which then follows as the subject: “A disease complex with a multifactorial etiology, BRD is a leading cause of mortality in calves.” Often the subject becomes a pronoun, as in “A disease complex with a multifactorial etiology, it is a leading cause of mortality in calves”, which needs an antecedent for “it” in the sentence before.
Fronting is a stylistic choice, with costs and benefits.
Benefits 

It states the category before the specifics. The reader learns what kind of thing the subject is, then what is said about it.
It joins two statements without a connecting verb such as “is” or “serves as”, so the sentence is shorter.
It puts a familiar description first and the new claim last, where the reader’s attention lands.

Costs 

The fronted phrase must describe the grammatical subject that follows. Otherwise it dangles: “A disease complex with a multifactorial etiology, mortality in calves is high” says that mortality is a disease complex.
The reader waits for the subject and verb, which runs against the advice to lead with the subject. A long fronted appositive delays them, and a reader may take the phrase for the subject (compare Avoid garden-path sentences).
The sentence no longer asserts the description as a main-clause claim, so the reader may treat it as background even when it is the point.
A pronoun subject (“it”) needs an antecedent in the previous sentence. A reader who cannot find it must stop to look.
It seems more formal and literary, which suits some venues and not others.

Guideline. Front an appositive when it is short, familiar to the reader, and describes the subject. Keep the plain “X is Y” form when the description is the new information the paper depends on, when it is long, or when the subject is a pronoun without a clear antecedent.







Example 8 (Plain and fronted forms)  

Plain: Bovine respiratory disease (BRD) is a disease complex with a multifactorial etiology and serves as a significant cause of mortality among preweaned calves and weaned cattle alike.
Fronted: A disease complex with a multifactorial etiology, BRD is a leading cause of mortality in both preweaned calves and weaned cattle.

The fronted version is shorter and puts the category first. It works here because “a disease complex with a multifactorial etiology” describes BRD, the subject that follows it, and the subject is named, not a pronoun. If the multifactorial etiology is what the paper is about, the plain form states it as a claim the reader can challenge, and is the better choice.






7 Put a comma before the last item of a list
In a list of three or more items, put a comma before the “and” or “or” that closes the list. This comma is called the serial comma, or the Oxford comma. With it, the reader sees where each item ends, and does not have to guess whether the last two items form a pair.
Write “the mean, the median, and the mode”, not “the mean, the median and the mode”.  The same holds when the items are long, are split across source lines, or contain math.







Example 9 (Adding the serial comma)  

❌ We compare the lasso, ridge regression and elastic net. 
✅ We compare the lasso, ridge regression, and elastic net.

In the first version, a reader can take “ridge regression and elastic net” as a single method that combines the two. The comma before “and” shows that there are three methods.




A list of two items takes no comma: “the mean and the median”. A phrase that opens a sentence is set off by its own comma, and it does not make a list: “In practice, the mean and the median agree.”
A line that must keep a list without the serial comma, such as a quotation or the ❌ half of an example, takes the marker <!-- check-serial-comma: allow -->.










 Back to top

title: Conciseness
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.


Concise writing conveys ideas efficiently, using only the words necessary to communicate meaning clearly. Every word should serve a purpose. Eliminate redundancy and verbosity. When you can express an idea in fewer words without losing meaning, do so.

1 Common ways to improve conciseness

Remove redundant phrases

“in order to” → “to”
“due to the fact that” → “because”
“at this point in time” → “now”
“a large number of” → “many”

Use the active voice (see Write in the active voice) 

“The experiment was conducted by the researchers” → “The researchers conducted the experiment”

Eliminate unnecessary qualifiers

“very”, “really”, “quite” often add little meaning

Replace wordy phrases with single words

“make a decision” → “decide”
“give consideration to” → “consider”
“is able to” → “can”


Remember: concise writing is not about making every sentence as short as possible, but about removing words that do not contribute to meaning or clarity. Keep a clause or a technical term when removing it would lose meaning or precision, and never replace an honest hedge with false confidence.


2 Make every word tell
Strunk’s rule 13 states the principle: “Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts.” He adds that this “requires not that the writer make all his sentences short, or that he avoid all detail and treat his subjects only in outline, but that he make every word tell” (Strunk 1920, rule 13).
Strunk’s examples of expressions that waste words:

“the question as to whether” → “whether”
“used for fuel purposes” → “used for fuel”
“in a hasty manner” → “hastily”
“owing to the fact that” → “since”
“the fact that he had not succeeded” → “his failure”
“His brother, who is a member of the same firm” → “His brother, a member of the same firm”

The same rule applies to statistical writing: “We conducted an analysis of the data to determine whether there is an association between smoking and lung cancer” becomes “We tested whether smoking is associated with lung cancer”.
The rule covers sentences as well as words. An interesting aside that does not serve the point costs the reader more than space. In experiments on a science lesson, adding such seductive details reduced what students recalled of the main explanation and how well they applied it to new problems (Harp and Mayer 1998).


3 Write in the active voice
Use the active voice unless you have a specific reason to use the passive. An active sentence names who did what, and it is usually shorter. A passive sentence can hide the actor, and the reader then has to guess who made the choice.
Choose the actor by who did the work:

Use “I” for what the author did, such as a choice the author made or a step in the author’s analysis. With several authors, use “we”.
Use “we” when the author and the reader work through an argument together, as in “we now compute the gradient”.


❌ The minimum was found exactly, and the model was chosen by eye.
✅ We found the minimum exactly, and we chose the model by eye. (The author and reader work through the example together.)
✅ I chose the model by eye, because the study had five points. (A single author reports a choice.)

Passive voice is the right choice in a few cases:

The actor is unknown or does not matter, as in “The samples were contaminated.”
The receiver of the action is the topic of the paragraph, and the sentence is easier to follow with it as the subject.
The actor would be a vague “someone” or “one”, and no real person or group acts.

When none of these applies, rewrite the sentence with an active verb.


4 Write about the ideas, not the document
A sentence about which part of the document holds a definition adds no content. State the idea and link the term, as Talk about the ideas, not the notes explains. The ✅ example below omits the link only because this guide has no page for the term.

❌ The statistics notes define the training error as the average loss on the fitted data.
✅ The training error is the average loss on the data used to fit the model.



5 Lead with the subject
Start a sentence with its subject, not a dependent clause or a fronted phrase. A leading clause makes the reader hold a condition before knowing what it conditions.

❌ When the sample size grows, the estimate becomes more precise.
✅ The estimate becomes more precise as the sample size grows.

A fronted phrase delays the subject in the same way. Move a phrase such as “in technical writing” or “in this study” after the noun it limits, unless it sets a scope that the whole paragraph depends on.

❌ In technical writing, a common cause of garden-path sentences is a missing that.
✅ A common cause of garden-path sentences in technical writing is a missing that.



6 Put the emphatic words at the end
The end of a sentence is the position the reader remembers. Strunk states the rule as “Place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end” (Strunk 1920, rule 18). Put the claim you want the reader to keep last, and put the qualifications, the citation and the filler before it. Gopen and Swan call the end of a sentence its stress position (Gopen and Swan 1990).

❌ The estimate becomes more precise as the sample size grows, in general.
✅ In general, the estimate becomes more precise as the sample size grows.



7 Start a sentence from what the reader already knows
Open each sentence with information that the reader already has, and end it with the new information. Readers connect a sentence to the text before it through its opening words. They understand a sentence faster when its known part clearly matches something already said (Haviland and Clark 1974). Gopen and Swan call the start of a sentence its topic position, and they advise putting the old information there and the new information in the stress position (Gopen and Swan 1990). A sentence that opens with a new idea makes the reader hold that idea until the words that connect it to the previous sentence arrive.

❌ The lasso sets some coefficients exactly to zero. Variable selection is the name for removing predictors from a model in this way.
✅ The lasso sets some coefficients exactly to zero. Setting a coefficient to zero removes its predictor from the model, so the lasso also selects variables.

In the ✅ version, the second sentence opens with the idea that the first sentence ended on, and ends with the new idea, variable selection. The subject of a sentence usually carries the known information, so this rule and Lead with the subject work together. The new information is usually also the part to emphasize, so Put the emphatic words at the end applies too.


8 Express coordinate ideas in parallel form
Items that play the same role in a sentence or a list take the same grammatical form. Strunk calls this parallel construction, and states the rule as “Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form” (Strunk 1920, rule 15). Put lists in bullet points applies the rule to the items of a list. The rule also holds inside one sentence, where a series joins verbs, noun phrases or adjectives and each item should be the same kind of phrase.

❌ The model is fast, accurate and has been validated.
✅ The model is fast, accurate and validated.



9 Limit complex sentence structures
A sentence with several nested dependent clauses forces the reader to hold each unfinished clause in mind until the sentence finally resolves. Compound sentences joined by coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or) are usually fine, and an occasional dependent clause is fine too; the problem is piling several of them into a single sentence.
When a sentence becomes hard to follow, split it into shorter sentences, each carrying one main idea.







Example 1 (Splitting an over-nested sentence)  

❌ Because the assay, which we had validated the previous year using samples that were collected before the outbreak began, produced results that, although noisy, were consistent with prior reports, we proceeded with the analysis.
✅ We had validated the assay the previous year, using samples collected before the outbreak began. Its results were noisy but consistent with prior reports, so we proceeded with the analysis.

The revised version breaks one deeply nested sentence into two and restores the natural chronological order (validation, then results, then decision), so the reader can absorb each idea before moving on.






10 Do not interrupt a clause with an aside
Do not put an aside between parts of a clause that belong together, whether the aside sits in parentheses or between commas. The reader has to hold the unfinished clause open until the aside ends. The parts that belong together include:

a subject and its verb;
a verb and its object;
two clauses joined by and or so.

Give the aside a sentence of its own, or move it after the clause it explains.

❌ The estimator, which assumes the errors are independent, is biased for these data.
✅ The estimator is biased for these data, because it assumes the errors are independent.

A long aside widens the gap further.

❌ The model has no minimizer (its second derivative is negative, so it decreases without limit as the step grows) and the theorem does not apply.
✅ The theorem does not apply, because it requires a positive second derivative. Instead, the model decreases without limit as the step grows, so it has no minimizer.

A short aside that only points to a source, such as “(Figure 2)”, can stay where it is.


11 Do not rule out readings no reader would make
A definition says what a term means. It does not need to list the things the term does not mean, unless a reader is likely to confuse the two. A disclaimer against a reading nobody would make costs the reader a sentence and can plant the confusion it was meant to prevent.







Example 2 (Dropping a needless disclaimer)  

❌ In this manuscript, TTE means target trial emulation. It does not mean effect of treatment on the treated.
✅ In this manuscript, TTE means target trial emulation.

In causal inference, the average effect of treatment on the treated is usually abbreviated ATT, so a reader is unlikely to read “TTE” that way. The second sentence introduces a meaning that the reader would not otherwise have considered.




Keep a disclaimer when the confusion is real. For example, if “CI” could mean confidence interval or cumulative incidence  in the same paper, say which one you mean each time.
A contrast you keep must not be a straw man. Say who holds the confusing reading, and cite a source that shows it, so the reader sees why the alternative needs ruling out. A bare “not X” leaves the reader to guess whether anyone reads the term as X.  If you cannot find a source or a reader who holds the reading, the contrast fails the test above, so remove it.







Example 3 (Explaining the contrast, or dropping it)  

❌ Statistics uses “predictor” for a feature, not for a model.
✅ Statistics uses “predictor” for a feature. Some machine learning texts use the same word for a fitted prediction function:  Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman call the averaged forest function “the random forest (regression) predictor” (Hastie et al. 2009, equation 15.2). In these notes, “predictor” always means a feature.

The first version rules out a reading without saying that anyone holds it. The second shows that the reading exists, with a source, and says which meaning the text uses. If no text used the word that way, the right revision would be to delete the clause “not for a model”.




The same test applies to explanations: explain what your intended readers do not already know, and leave out what they do. A methods section for statisticians does not need to define a p-value; a report for clinicians might.


12 Avoid double negatives
A double negative states a claim by denying its opposite, as in these phrases:

“not uncommon”
“not unlikely”
“not inconsistent with”

The reader has to cancel the two negatives to recover the claim, and the result is often vaguer than the writer intended. State the claim directly. If you mean something weaker than the direct claim, say what the weaker claim is.
A single negative is fine. “We did not reject the null hypothesis” denies one thing, and it is the standard wording for a test result.







Example 4 (Stating a claim directly)  

❌ The association was not inconsistent with a dose-response relationship.
✅ The association was consistent with a dose-response relationship.
✅ The data do not rule out a dose-response relationship, but they do not support one either.

Writers usually choose “not inconsistent with” to hedge “consistent with”. The first rewrite drops the hedge; the second says what the hedge was for. Choose the one you mean.






13 Write about the subject, not about the text
Some sentences describe the document instead of its subject. They do one of these things:

announce that a point is coming;
rank a point;
comment on how a point changes what follows.

Each one makes the reader read a sentence before reaching the content it promises. State the content directly. Rhetorical reflexes lists related signpost phrases, such as “it is worth noting that”.







Example 5 (Replacing a sentence about the text)  

❌ One trap worth naming: the sample excludes people who moved.
✅ The sample excludes people who moved.
❌ The most important point is that the survey was voluntary.
✅ The survey was voluntary.
❌ One documented detail changes how the rest of this section reads: the survey was voluntary.
✅ The survey was voluntary, so the estimates apply only to people who chose to respond.

In the third pair, the rewrite states what the detail changes instead of saying that it changes something.






14 Let a self-describing link stand alone
A URL often shows the name of what it points to and where that thing lives. When it does, do not also spell out that name or host around the link. The reader would read the same facts twice.







Example 6 (Dropping prose that repeats a URL)  

❌ For an example, see my public notes site Morrison-Lab/sds on GitHub (https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/sds).
✅ For an example, see https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/sds.

The URL already says that the site is on GitHub and that the repository is Morrison-Lab/sds.




Keep a descriptive label when the URL does not show what it points to, such as a DOI or a shortened link.


15 Keep the writer out of the way
Mention yourself only where a sentence needs an actor, such as a request, an offer, or a decision you made. Elsewhere, make the subject of the sentence the thing the reader cares about. Extra references to the writer turn attention from the content to the person.







Example 7 (Moving the focus from the writer to the subject)  

❌ I tested this in a small private project, and I found that CI works well.
✅ CI works well in a small private test project.
❌ My build and review tools run on cloud services.
✅ The build and review tools run on cloud services.

A request still needs its actor: “Could the space be increased, or would you allow me to register my own runner?”  keeps “me” because the request is about the writer’s runner.






16 Do not overexplain
Say what the reader needs, and stop. Cut a qualifier, a restatement or a reason that the words before it already imply.







Example 8 (Cutting a clause the term already implies)  

❌ Estimated mean: the estimated value of the mean, whether or not it is a mean of an outcome.
✅ Estimated mean: the estimated value of the mean.

The first version adds a clause that “the mean” already covers. The second is complete.






17 Put lists in bullet points
A list of three or more phrases, written inline and separated by commas, makes the reader count commas to find where each item ends. Write it as a bullet list instead, introduced by a sentence ending in a colon. Use a numbered list when the items are steps done in order.
A run of parallel sentences is a list too, even with only two items. The common case is a set of resources, such as videos or readings, where each sentence names one resource and links to it. Put each sentence in its own bullet, so the reader sees how many resources there are and where each one starts.
A series introduced by a colon is a list too, even with only two items, when the items hold math or links. Write each item as a bullet, and display any equation the reader must remember (see Example 13).
A case analysis is a parallel run too. Write one bullet per case, and begin each with a bold label that names the case.
Say whether a list is exhaustive or exemplary. Ezra Morrison stated the rule on 2026-11-04:

always specify whether a list is exhaustive (with a lead-in like “X consists of the following categories:”) versus exemplary (lead in with “for example:”, “including:”, end with “etc”, or similar).

Without a marker, the reader cannot tell whether an item left off the list is missing from the topic or only from the list (see Example 14).
Bullet lists matter most on slides, where a reader scans a list rather than reading it as a sentence. The rule is one case of a broader preference for more structure: when content has a shape, show that shape in the markup.
A few mechanics to keep in mind when writing a bullet list:

Keep the items grammatically parallel, so each one completes the introducing sentence the same way.
Leave a blank line before the list; without it, Markdown reads the list as part of the paragraph above.
Keep a short series of single words inline, such as “R, Julia, or Python”.








Example 9 (Turning an inline list into bullet points)  

❌ Machine learning combines data to learn from, statistics to say what a finite sample of data supports, and optimization to find the model that fits the data best.
✅ Machine learning combines three components:

data to learn from;
statistics to say what a finite sample of data supports;
optimization to find the model that fits the data best.


The revised version puts each component on its own line, so the reader sees at a glance that there are three.











Example 10 (Turning a run of resource sentences into bullet points)  

❌ Hastie and Tibshirani extend least squares to several predictors. Starmer explains multiple regression.
✅ Videos:

Hastie and Tibshirani extend least squares to several predictors.
Starmer explains multiple regression.


For the video notes this example comes from, see the DATA 571 chapter on linear regression. Each bullet holds one video, so the reader can pick one without parsing the paragraph.











Example 11 (Turning inline steps into a numbered list)  

❌ k-means starts with \(k\) group centers, assigns each point to its nearest center, moves each center to the mean of its points, and repeats until the assignments stop changing.
✅ k-means starts with \(k\) group centers and repeats two steps until the assignments stop changing:

assign each point to its nearest center;
move each center to the mean of its points.


The numbers show the order of the steps, and the loop condition moves into the introducing sentence.











Example 12 (Turning a paragraph of cases into bullet points)  

❌ At \(z = 0\) the slope is \(\dexpitf{0} = 1/4\). At \(z = 2\) it is \(\dexpitf{2} \approx 0.105\). At \(z = -2\) it is \(\dexpitf{-2} \approx 0.105\).
✅ The slope \(\dexpitf{z}\) at three values of \(z\):

\(z = 0\): \(\dexpitf{0} = 1/4\).
\(z = 2\): \(\dexpitf{2} \approx 0.105\).
\(z = -2\): \(\dexpitf{-2} \approx 0.105\).


The labels let the reader find a case at a glance, and the bullets show that there are three.











Example 13 (Turning a colon series with math into bullet points)  

❌ Derive the other two formulations: minimizing the negative log-likelihood \(\argmin_{\vcoef}\ \sb{-\llik(\vcoef)}\), and empirical risk minimization \(\argmin_{\vcoef}\empriskf{\vcoef}\) with \(\emprisk = \tfrac1\nobs\sum_i \lossf{\outvar_i, \prob_i}\).
✅ Derive the other two formulations:

minimizing the negative log-likelihood, \(\argmin_{\vcoef}\ \sb{-\llik(\vcoef)}\);
empirical risk minimization, \(\argmin_{\vcoef}\empriskf{\vcoef}\), with \[\emprisk = \tfrac1\nobs\sum_i \lossf{\outvar_i, \prob_i}.\]


Each bullet holds one formulation, and the definition of the empirical risk is displayed rather than buried in the sentence.











Example 14 (Marking a list as exhaustive or exemplary)  

❌ The metrics computed from a confusion matrix are:

accuracy;
sensitivity;
specificity.

✅ A confusion matrix for a binary classifier consists of the following four cells:

true positives;
false positives;
false negatives;
true negatives.

✅ Metrics computed from a confusion matrix include:

accuracy;
sensitivity;
specificity;
etc.


The first lead-in reads as exhaustive, yet a confusion matrix yields more metrics than the three listed. The second lead-in says that the four cells are the whole set, and the third says that its list is a sample.






18 Write to communicate, not to impress
Many rules in this chapter serve one aim: the reader should reach your meaning without extra work. A long word, a nested sentence or a crowded paragraph can make a text sound more formal, but it can add work for the reader without adding to the meaning. So at each level of the text, choose the plainest form that still carries the full meaning:

for words, see Word choice;
for sentences, see Limit complex sentence structures;
for paragraphs, give each one a single topic, as Keep a predictable structure says;
for mathematics, see Making expressions concise.








Example 15 (Rewriting a sentence written to sound formal)  

❌ It is imperative to acknowledge that, notwithstanding the methodological constraints that were encountered in the course of the study, the findings that were obtained are indicative of a substantial association between the exposure and the outcome.
✅ Despite the limits of the study’s methods, the results suggest a substantial association between the exposure and the outcome.

The ✅ version drops “It is imperative to acknowledge that”, which only says that the next claim matters. It replaces “notwithstanding” with “despite” and “are indicative of” with “suggest”, as Replacing unnecessary jargon does for single words. It puts the noun phrases in plainer words too: “methodological constraints” becomes “the limits of the study’s methods”, and “findings” becomes “results”. It also removes the relative clauses “that were encountered in the course of the study” and “that were obtained”, because a study’s constraints are ones it faced, and its findings are ones it obtained.






19 Examples of concise writing
Many effective writers throughout history have exemplified the principle of conciseness.
Julius Caesar’s Commentarii and phrases like “Veni, vidi, vici” demonstrate the power of brevity (Wikipedia contributors 2026b).
Ernest Hemingway was known for his spare, direct prose style. His short sentences and simple words conveyed complex ideas and emotions without unnecessary embellishment (Wikipedia contributors 2026a).











 Back to topReferences

NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.
Clichés recur across unrelated documents, so they make writing seem generic and unconsidered, even when the underlying content is sound.
AI writing assistants often produce these patterns in clusters, and many readers have learned to treat the patterns as signs that a draft was generated and to doubt that its author checked it.
Human drafts use the same patterns, so this chapter is for any writer, including anyone editing a draft that an assistant helped write. It catalogs the most common clichés so you can remove them.

2.1 Overused vocabulary

Whole phrases recur too. “In today’s fast-paced world”, “it is important to note that”, and “plays a vital role in” add length without content; delete them and start with the actual point. Two more families recur, and each member should give way to the literal claim:

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
2.2 Rhetorical reflexes
Writers reach for a few sentence shapes by reflex, whether or not the content calls for them.
The most recognizable is the not just X, but Y antithesis. It promises a profound contrast and usually delivers a hollow one.







Example 1 (The “not just X, but Y” reflex)  

❌ This method is not just fast — it is transformative.
✅ This method runs in half the time of the previous approach.

The plain version makes a concrete, verifiable claim. The antithesis frame makes none.




Other reflexes to watch for:

Mechanical lists of three. Three parallel items appear whether or not three is the right count. Use the number of items the point actually needs.
Signpost filler. Phrases like “it is worth noting that” and “importantly” announce a point instead of making it. Cut them and state the point directly.
Hedging stacks. “May potentially suggest” and “could possibly indicate” pile up qualifiers. Keep one honest hedge; drop the rest.
Hollow summaries. A closing paragraph that opens with “in conclusion” and only restates what you just said adds nothing. End on a real point.


2.2.1 Say what it is before what it is not
When a sentence needs both a positive claim and a denial, state the positive claim first. The reader learns what the subject is before being told what to rule out, and the denial then attaches to a claim already made. Opening with the denial makes the reader carry an unsupported denial until the second clause arrives.







Example 2 (Positive claim, then denial)  

❌ The padding is not a convention, it is an identity.
✅ The padding is an identity, not a convention.

The first version says “not a convention” before the reader knows what the padding is, then repeats the subject and verb to supply the claim. The second version states the claim once and ends on the contrast.
The order matters even when the sentence stays grammatical:

❌ The padding is not a convention but an identity.
✅ The padding is an identity, not a convention.

Both are correct sentences; the second puts the claim first. For the first pair, see the linear regression chapter of lds.




Often the denial can be cut. Keep it only when the reader might plausibly believe the rejected reading, as with a convention versus an identity. A denial that rejects a view nobody holds is the reframe (see Clichéd sentence shapes) in miniature: cut it and keep the claim.

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
2.3 Clichéd sentence shapes
Beyond the antithesis, clichéd drafts lean on a set of sentence shapes that stage a point instead of stating it.







Example 3 (A staged point)  

❌ It can read like a definition that says nothing. Its use is in what it forces you to name: a project that cannot say what its \(E\), \(T\) and \(P\) are has not yet stated a machine learning problem.
✅ A machine learning problem is stated only when its experience \(E\), task \(T\) and performance measure \(P\) are named.

The first version packs six clichés into two sentences:

an objection raised only to be knocked down;
“It” and “Its” in place of “the definition”;
a definition that “forces” the reader, as if it were a person;
“you” addressing the reader;
a point withheld until after a colon;
a closing aphorism.

The second version states the claim once.




Watch for these shapes:

The straw objection. A doubt raised only to be answered (“It may seem trivial. In fact, …”). This is the antithesis spread over two sentences.
The personified abstraction. A definition, method or result that “forces”, “invites”, “demands” or “asks” something of the reader, or a mathematical object that “recommends”, “knows” or “wants” something. Name who does what, and state the condition the phrase hides (Avoid vague and metaphorical language).
The colon reveal. A setup, then a colon, then the point. Lead with the point.
The answered rhetorical question. “The result? A faster fit.” or “Why does this matter? Because …”. State the result.
The throat-clearing lead-in. “Here’s the thing:”, “Here’s why:”, “The key is”, “Put simply,”. Delete the lead-in.
The announced claim. “It is what makes … valid”, “That is what …”, “This is what …”, and “What the standing grant removes is the need to ask”. The sentence points at its own claim before making it. Make the claim directly: “It is what makes sums over countably infinite partitions valid” becomes “It makes sums over countably infinite partitions valid”, and “What the standing grant removes is the need to ask” becomes “The standing grant removes the need to ask”. The same holds for a subject followed by “is what” and a verb, and for a tail of “, which is why” or “, which is what”: “The risk is what says how a model does on neighborhoods outside the sample” becomes “The risk measures how well a model predicts neighborhoods outside the sample”, “Solving the equation is what this course calls learning” becomes “This course calls solving the equation learning”, “No label was used, which is why the task is unsupervised” becomes “No label was used, so the task is unsupervised”, and “The step is cheap, which is what makes it affordable” becomes “The step is cheap, so it is affordable”. Keep a “, which is why” tail only where a real reason follows that the reader would not guess.
The reframe. “X isn’t about Y; it’s about Z”, “The question isn’t X, it’s Y”, and “not because X, but because Y”. Say what X is about.
Fragment emphasis. “Simple. Fast. Reliable.” Write a sentence with a subject and a verb.
The editorializing tail. A trailing participial clause that comments on the sentence: “, highlighting the importance of …”, “, ensuring that …”, “, making it ideal for …”. End the sentence at its claim.
The inflated copula. “Serves as”, “stands as” and “acts as” where “is” says the same.
The range frame. “From X to Y” listing two extremes instead of naming the scope.
The audience frame. “Whether you’re a student or a researcher, …”. Drop it.
The restatement. “In other words, …” repeating the previous sentence. Keep the clearer of the two.
The closing aphorism. A one-line verdict at the end of a paragraph: “And that’s the point.”, “Simple as that.”, “… has not yet stated a problem.” End on the last piece of content.
Sincerity intensifiers. “Genuinely”, “truly”, “actually”, “really” and “crucially” used to sound earnest. Cut them.
Chained connectors. “Furthermore”, “Moreover” and “Additionally” opening consecutive sentences. Most can go; the order already signals addition.
Assistant chatter. “Let’s dive in”, “Let’s unpack this”, “Great question” and “I hope this helps” belong in a chat window, not a document.

Four more habits blur the referent or delay the claim. Other chapters cover each:

a demonstrative standing in for its referent (Demonstrative pronouns);
the word “thing” (Say which thing);
a dependent clause opening a sentence (Lead with the subject);
informal idioms (Avoid vague and metaphorical language).

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
2.4 Formatting habits
Some clichés are typographic rather than verbal.

The em-dash as a default connector. Some writers, and many AI drafts, use the em-dash to join almost any two clauses. Vary your punctuation: a period, a comma, or a semicolon is often the better fit.
Bold-leading bullets everywhere. A **Term:** explanation bullet is fine once, but applying the pattern to every list turns it into a tic. Use it when the label earns emphasis, plain bullets otherwise.
Emoji section headers. Emoji in headings signal a blog post, not a scientific document. Leave them out.
Uniform paragraph rhythm. Paragraphs of near-identical length, each three or four sentences, seem monotonous. Let paragraph length follow the ideas.

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
2.5 Tone
The last group of clichés is about register.

Promotional language. Words like “powerful”, “game-changing”, and “cutting-edge” sell rather than inform. Describe what the thing does and let the reader judge.
Reflexive both-sides framing. Tacking “however, it is important to consider the other side” onto every claim signals caution without adding content. Use a hedge when the evidence is genuinely mixed, not by habit.
Vague universals. “Studies show” and “experts agree”, with no specific source or number, are clichés precisely because they dodge the evidence. Name the study and give the number, as the Citations and evidence chapter recommends.

title: Citations and evidence
text: Every claim in scientific writing should be supported by either citations to relevant sources or direct evidence from data or experiments. This principle is fundamental to maintaining credibility, enabling verification, and building on the accumulated knowledge of the scientific community.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
2.1 Empirical claims
Claims about observable phenomena or data should be supported by:

Direct presentation of the data (tables, figures, statistical analyses)
Citations to published studies that collected the relevant data
Description of experimental methods that generated the evidence
Links to publicly accessible datasets

title: Citations and evidence
text:
2.2 Theoretical claims
Claims about concepts, models, or interpretations should be supported by:

Citations to papers that developed or validated the theory
Logical arguments with clearly stated premises
Mathematical derivations or proofs
References to review articles that synthesize relevant theoretical work

title: Citations and evidence
text:
2.3 Methodological claims
Claims about appropriate methods or best practices should be supported by:

Citations to methodological papers or textbooks
Empirical evidence of method performance
Expert consensus statements
Validation studies

title: Citations and evidence
text:
2.4 Common knowledge
Not every statement requires citation. Well-established facts that are common knowledge within your field (for example, “DNA is a double helix” in molecular biology) can be stated without citation. However, when in doubt, provide a citation—over-citing is preferable to under-citing.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
3.1 “Trivial” and “trivially”
“Trivial” and “trivially” usually work the same way: they announce that a step is too small to write down, which relieves the writer of writing it down. Treat them as a prompt to check the step, and to write it out if it takes only a line.
The word has one defensible use, which is describing how a general expression reduces to a simpler one in a special case. For example, a weighted average reduces to an ordinary average when all of the weights are equal. Even in that use, “minimal case” or “degenerate case” names the situation more precisely, and avoids the dismissive tone that “trivial” carries.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
5.1 Peer review
Peer-reviewed publications in reputable journals have undergone expert scrutiny. This doesn’t guarantee correctness, but it provides a baseline level of quality control.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
5.2 Reputation of authors and institutions
Work from recognized experts and well-regarded institutions tends to be more reliable, though this should not be the sole criterion.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
5.3 Replication and consensus
Findings that have been replicated by independent groups or that represent scientific consensus are more trustworthy than isolated claims.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
5.4 Transparency and reproducibility
Studies that:

Clearly describe their methods
Share their data and code
Disclose potential conflicts of interest
Have been successfully reproduced by others

are more trustworthy than those lacking these features.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
5.5 Preprints and non-peer-reviewed sources
Preprints can be valuable for accessing cutting-edge research, but they have not undergone peer review. When citing preprints:

Note that they are preprints
Check whether a peer-reviewed version has since been published
Exercise extra scrutiny of the methods and conclusions

title: Citations and evidence
text:
5.6 Sources to generally avoid
Some sources typically lack the rigor needed for scientific writing:

Wikipedia and general encyclopedias as the only source for a claim (cite them beside the primary source, as Cite Wikipedia, beside the primary source explains)
Popular press articles about scientific findings (cite the original research instead)
Blogs and social media posts (unless discussing public discourse or documenting specific claims made in those venues)
Predatory or pay-to-publish journals without genuine peer review
Retracted papers

title: Citations and evidence
text:
24.1 Poor (unsupported claim)

Machine learning models often perform poorly on small datasets.

Problem: This claim is stated as fact without any support.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
24.2 Better (citation provided)

Machine learning models often perform poorly on small datasets (Vapnik 1998; Hawkins 2004).

Improvement: Citations provide evidence for the claim.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
24.3 Best (citation with context)

Machine learning models often perform poorly on small datasets. Vapnik (1998) showed that the generalization error of learning algorithms typically decreases as training set size increases, and Hawkins (2004) demonstrated that complex models are particularly prone to overfitting when trained on limited data (Vapnik 1998; Hawkins 2004).

Improvement: The specific support each citation provides is explained.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
24.4 Poor (irrelevant citation)

Python is the most popular programming language for data science (Knuth 1984).

Problem: Knuth’s 1984 paper on literate programming doesn’t address Python or data science.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
24.5 Better (relevant citation)

Python is the most popular programming language for data science (Stack Overflow 2024).

Improvement: The citation is to a current survey of programming language usage.

title: Defining terms clearly
text: Clear definitions are essential to effective scientific writing. Every specialized term should have an explicit, concise definition before its first use. Readers should not need to search for the meaning of a term or infer it from context alone. For example:

title: Defining terms clearly
text:
8.1 Using theorem environments in Quarto
When writing mathematical or technical content in Quarto, use theorem environments to demarcate and highlight the structure of your content. These environments provide consistent formatting, automatic numbering, and cross-reference capabilities.
Quarto provides built-in theorem environments including:

#thm- for theorems
#lem- for lemmas
#cor- for corollaries
#prp- for propositions
#cnj- for conjectures
#def- for definitions
#exm- for examples
#exr- for exercises
#sol- for solutions, named after their exercise (#exr-foo and #sol-foo)
#rem- for remarks

See the Quarto documentation on theorems and proofs for complete details.
Example syntax:
::: {#thm-pythagorean}

## Pythagorean theorem

In a right triangle,
the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares of the other two sides:

$$a^2 + b^2 = c^2.$$

:::
This produces automatically numbered output like “Theorem 2.1 (Pythagorean theorem)” and can be referenced elsewhere in your document using @thm-pythagorean.

Theorem 1 (Pythagorean theorem) In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares of the other two sides:
